clinicalScope: Community‑acquired pneumonia in children and adults presenting to low‑resource East African hospitals
subject: Medicine
summary: Pneumonia is an infection that fills the tiny air sacs of the lungs with fluid, causing fever, cough and difficulty breathing. In East African district hospitals the most common causes are bacteria like Streptococcus pneumoniae and aspiration of oral contents, and doctors must often decide with limited tests.

sections.p: Pneumonia is infection of the lung parenchyma (alveoli and interstitium) leading to consolidation – air‑filled spaces become filled with inflammatory exudate.
b: Global cause of ~15 % of all deaths; highest mortality in children <5 yr and adults >65 yr in low‑resource settings.
In East Africa, incidence ≈ 0.5–1 episode per 100 person‑years, with seasonal peaks during the rainy months.
Male predominance modest (≈55 % of cases) due to higher exposure to indoor smoke and occupational dust.
Case‑fatality in district hospitals ranges 5–12 % without timely antibiotics.

sections.h: Causes and risk factors, most likely first
sections.p: In the described setting bacterial pathogens dominate, but local risk factors shape the aetiology.
b: Streptococcus pneumoniae – most frequent, especially in children >2 yr and adults with HIV.
Aspiration of oropharyngeal contents – common after stroke, alcohol intoxication, seizures; right lower lobe predilection.
Haemophilus influenzae – especially in children with malnutrition or recent viral illness.
Staphylococcus aureus – post‑influenza or skin infection; higher risk of necrotising disease.
Mycoplasma pneumoniae – atypical, milder, more common in school‑aged children and young adults.
HIV infection – predisposes to bacterial, Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.
Indoor air pollution (biomass fuel) – chronic bronchial irritation increases bacterial colonisation.

sections.p: Inhaled organisms or aspirated material trigger an innate immune response that fills alveoli with protein‑rich exudate, impairing gas exchange.
b: Microbial adhesion to alveolar epithelium → release of cytokines (IL‑1, TNF‑α).
Neutrophil influx → capillary leakage, fibrin deposition, formation of consolidation.
Ventilation‑perfusion mismatch → hypoxaemia; shunt physiology when alveoli are completely filled.
Systemic inflammatory response may progress to sepsis if bacterial load is high.

sections.p: Typical presentation is abrupt and systemic, but in low‑resource settings atypical features are common.
b: Fever ≥38 °C, chills, rigors.
Productive cough; sputum may be rust‑coloured (blood) or purulent.
Pleuritic chest pain worsening on inspiration.
Dyspnoea with respiratory rate ≥30 /min (adult) or ≥60 /min (child).
General malaise, anorexia, sometimes confusion in the elderly.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and physical guide severity assessment and choice of investigations.
b: Ask about recent viral illness, sick contacts, HIV status, smoking, indoor smoke exposure, dysphagia or recent vomiting.
Examine for: tachypnoea, use of accessory muscles, cyanosis, fever, and mental status changes.
Auscultation: bronchial breath sounds over consolidation, crackles (rales), egophony (nasal quality of voice).
Percussion: dullness over the affected lobe; fremitus increased.
Check for pleural effusion: dullness with shifting dullness when patient sits up.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic pneumonia on history or exam must be considered, especially where diagnostics are limited.
b: Pulmonary tuberculosis – chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats; often upper‑lobe infiltrates.
Acute bronchitis – cough without focal consolidation, normal chest exam.
Heart failure – bilateral crackles, peripheral oedema, cardiomegaly on X‑ray.
Pulmonary embolism – sudden dyspnoea, pleuritic pain, clear lungs on exam.
Lung cancer – weight loss, persistent localized mass, often in smokers.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Use a step‑wise approach; when a test is unavailable, rely on clinical scoring.

t.b: Is there a new infiltrate? – Presence confirms consolidation; lobar pattern suggests typical bacteria, interstitial pattern suggests atypical or viral.
What is the white cell count? – WCC >12 ×10⁹/L with neutrophilia supports bacterial infection; lymphocytosis may suggest viral/atypical.

t.a: Sputum Gram stain / culture (if patient can expectorate)
t.b: Which organism dominates? – Helps narrow antibiotic choice; Gram‑positive diplococci → S. pneumoniae.
SpO₂ < 90 % on room air? – Indicates need for supplemental oxygen and possible inpatient care.
Is antigen detected? – Positive test confirms pneumococcal aetiology, useful when sputum unavailable.

sections.p: CURB‑65 and the WHO Integrated Management of Adolescent and Adult Illness (IMAI) score guide admission decisions.
b: CURB‑65 ≥2 → consider hospitalisation; ≥3 → intensive care.
IMAI danger signs: respiratory rate >30/min (adult) or >60/min (child), SpO₂ <90 %, inability to drink, altered consciousness.
Assess comorbidities (HIV, heart disease) that raise risk.
Document PaO₂/FiO₂ if arterial blood gas available; <200 mmHg indicates severe disease.

sections.p: Co‑existing conditions frequently alter presentation and management.
b: HIV infection – higher likelihood of atypical organisms; need broader coverage (e.g., add cotrimoxazole for P. jirovecii if CD4 <200).
Malnutrition – blunted fever, lower WCC, higher mortality.
Concurrent malaria – overlapping fever; malaria test required before attributing all fever to pneumonia.
Recent antibiotic use – may mask typical sputum findings, increase resistance risk.

sections.p: Treat the pathogen, support oxygenation, and monitor for deterioration.
b: First dose of empiric antibiotic within 1 hour of diagnosis.
Oxygen to keep SpO₂ ≥ 94 % (≥ 90 % in COPD).
Hydration, antipyretics, and chest physiotherapy for sputum clearance.
Re‑evaluate at 48 h; switch to oral route if clinically improving.

sections.p: Early recognition of complications prevents mortality.
b: Empyema – pleuritic pain, fever, pleural fluid pH < 7.2, glucose < 40 mg/dL; requires thoracentesis and drainage.
Lung abscess – cavitary lesion >2 cm on imaging, foul‑smelling sputum; treat prolonged antibiotics and consider surgical drainage.
Septic shock – MAP < 65 mmHg despite fluids, cold extremities, altered mental status; initiate aggressive fluid resuscitation and vasopressors.
Respiratory failure – rising PaCO₂, falling PaO₂; need high‑flow oxygen or non‑invasive ventilation.

sections.p: Children, pregnant women, and HIV‑positive patients need tailored approaches.
b: Infants <2 months – consider viral (RSV) and bacterial (Group B Strep); give ampicillin plus gentamicin.
Pregnancy – avoid tetracyclines; use amoxicillin or ceftriaxone; monitor for pre‑term labour.
HIV with CD4 < 200 – add cotrimoxazole prophylaxis and consider TMP‑SMX for P. jirovecii if diffuse bilateral infiltrates.
Sickle cell disease – higher risk of pneumococcal infection; ensure pneumococcal vaccination and give high‑dose penicillin.

sections.p: Most patients recover with timely therapy; follow‑up ensures resolution and vaccination.
b: Re‑check clinical status at 48–72 h; if no improvement, reassess diagnosis and antibiotics.
Chest X‑ray repeat at 2 weeks if persistent fever or cough.
Vaccinate against Streptococcus pneumoniae (PCV13 for children, PPSV23 for adults >65 yr or high‑risk).
Promote hand hygiene, reduce indoor smoke, and ensure HIV testing and treatment.

sections.p: Interpretation pitfalls are common in low‑resource settings.
b: Normal WCC does not exclude bacterial pneumonia in HIV or malnourished patients.
Chest X‑ray may be falsely negative early in disease; rely on clinical criteria.
CRP can be elevated in malaria; use malaria rapid test to differentiate.
Sputum Gram stain may show normal flora; do not withhold antibiotics if clinical picture fits.

whenToSeekHelp: Respiratory rate > 30/min (adult) or > 60/min (child) with inability to speak full sentences
Systolic blood pressure < 90 mmHg or MAP < 65 mmHg
Persistent high fever > 39 °C despite antipyretics for > 48 h

faq.q: Why is amoxicillin preferred over macrolides in most East African patients?
faq.a: Local resistance data show low macrolide resistance but high penicillin susceptibility; amoxicillin is cheap, widely available, and covers the most common pathogen, S. pneumoniae.

faq.q: Can a normal chest X‑ray rule out pneumonia?
faq.a: No. Early infiltrates may be invisible; clinical signs and severity scores guide treatment even when the film is normal.

faq.q: When should I add anaerobic coverage?
faq.a: If the history suggests aspiration (e.g., recent vomiting, alcohol intoxication, neurological impairment) or if sputum is foul‑smelling, add metronidazole or clindamycin.

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with HIV (CD4 150) presents with fever, cough and pleuritic chest pain; what initial antibiotics would you choose and why? — Amoxicillin plus metronidazole for typical/aspiration coverage; consider adding TMP‑SMX if P. jirovecii suspected because CD4 < 200.

A child aged 3 years has a respiratory rate of 68/min, fever 38.5 °C, and crackles over the right lower lung; chest X‑ray unavailable. How do you decide on admission? — Use WHO IMCI criteria: fast breathing plus chest indrawing or danger sign → admit for IV antibiotics and oxygen.

Explain how CURB‑65 is calculated and how it influences disposition. — Assign one point each for Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate ≥30/min, Blood pressure (systolic <90 mmHg or diastolic ≤60 mmHg), Age ≥65 yr; ≥2 points → hospitalise, ≥3 → consider ICU.

A patient on day 3 of ceftriaxone develops pleuritic pain and a new dullness on percussion; pleural fluid analysis shows pH 7.1, glucose 30 mg/dL, neutrophil predominance. What is the diagnosis and next step? — Empyema; insert chest tube drainage and continue antibiotics.

Why is a sputum Gram stain of normal flora not sufficient to stop antibiotics in a patient with classic pneumonia signs? — In low‑resource settings, sputum quality may be poor; clinical syndrome and severity guide therapy regardless of culture.

Describe the pathophysiological reason for hypoxaemia in lobar pneumonia. — Consolidated alveoli are filled with exudate, eliminating ventilation while perfusion continues, creating a right‑to‑left shunt and lowering arterial oxygen.

A 70‑year‑old woman with hypertension presents with confusion, RR 32, BP 85/50, urea 9 mmol/L. What is her CURB‑65 score and management? — Score 4 (confusion, urea, RR, BP); admit to high‑dependency unit, start IV broad‑spectrum antibiotics and aggressive fluid resuscitation.
When is it appropriate to use doxycycline instead of amoxicillin? — When atypical organisms are suspected (young adult, dry cough, no lobar consolidation) or when penicillin allergy exists.

What are the key differences between aspiration pneumonia and typical bacterial pneumonia on imaging? — Aspiration often shows right lower‑lobe infiltrate, may be patchy or cavitary; typical bacterial pneumonia shows lobar consolidation.

A patient with malaria test positive and also meets pneumonia criteria. How do you prioritize treatment? — Treat both simultaneously; give antimalarial therapy and start empiric antibiotics because co‑infection is common and delaying antibiotics increases mortality.

Explain why pulse oximetry is preferred over arterial blood gas in district hospitals. — It is non‑invasive, rapid, requires no laboratory, and provides a reliable surrogate for oxygenation to guide oxygen therapy.

What vaccination strategies reduce community‑acquired pneumonia burden in East Africa? — Routine infant PCV13, adult PPSV23 for >65 yr or chronic disease, and influenza vaccination for high‑risk groups.
